opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the offense-defense balance in biology is not a fixed property of the technology. It's something we shape through the choices we make about what we build, who gets access, and where we invest. So rather than asking "will AI favor attackers or defenders?" as if it's a law of nature, I find it more useful to ask: what levers do we actually have, and are we pulling them?

Right now, I'd say biology has a structural asymmetry that worries me. On the offense side, you only need to succeed once, and many of the hard steps are about knowledge and troubleshooting, which is exactly where general-purpose AI models are getting better. On the defense side, you need surveillance, diagnostics, countermeasures, manufacturing capacity, and distribution, and all of that has to work at scale, under time pressure, across jurisdictions. That's an enormous coordination problem, and AI doesn't automatically solve coordination problems.

So how do you shift it? I think about it in a few layers.

The first is at the model and tool level: making sure frontier developers evaluate for meaningful biological uplift before release, and that safeguards scale with capability. That includes being thoughtful about specialized biological design tools, not just chatbots, because those raise different questions about access and verification.

The second layer is chokepoints in the physical world. Knowledge is getting cheaper, but turning knowledge into something dangerous still runs through materials and equipment. Universal DNA synthesis screening, customer verification, and screening built into benchtop synthesizers are some of the most robust interventions we have, because they don't depend on predicting exactly what a model might say.

The third layer is deliberately accelerating defensive applications. AI can genuinely help with early detection, things like metagenomic sequencing of wastewater or air, faster characterization of novel pathogens, faster vaccine and therapeutic design, and broad-spectrum countermeasures. If we funded these with the same urgency that goes into capabilities, we'd be in a much better place. Differential technology development, essentially: speed up the things that protect us relative to the things that endanger us.

And the last layer is resilience that doesn't depend on knowing the threat in advance. Better indoor air, far-UVC, stockpiles of next-generation PPE. These are boring, but they're pathogen-agnostic, and that matters when you can't anticipate what's coming.

The honest answer is that none of these alone is sufficient. But together, they can make the world meaningfully harder to harm, and that's the goal: not perfect prevention, but raising the cost of attack while lowering the cost of defense.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask what we can do to make defensive capabilities improve faster than offensive ones. An AI system that helps us understand biology could support vaccine development, but it could also lower some of the barriers to misuse. So making the tools more capable doesn’t, by itself, tell us which side benefits more.

I would think about this in layers. One is reducing opportunities for misuse: evaluating systems for dangerous capabilities, putting appropriate safeguards around access, and strengthening screening of DNA synthesis orders. Another is investing in the things that let us detect and respond to an outbreak quickly—surveillance, diagnostics, and the ability to develop and manufacture countermeasures.

And the practical deployment really matters. A promising model for designing vaccines is useful, but its defensive value depends on whether we can validate the result, manufacture it, and get it to people in time. Those are institutional and logistical problems as much as computational ones.

So I wouldn’t assume that AI will naturally favor defense. We need to deliberately build the infrastructure that turns scientific advances into protection, while checking whether our safeguards actually reduce the opportunities for harm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to avoid treating the offense-defense balance as a fixed property of AI. It depends on the capability we're talking about, who has access to it, and the environment in which it's deployed.

For biology, there's a distinction between helping someone understand a dangerous process and enabling them to carry it out. Information matters, but so do access to materials, equipment, practical expertise, and the ability to troubleshoot experiments. So we should ask where AI actually removes a bottleneck, and whether we can put effective safeguards at that point.

On the defensive side, we want to make it easier to detect outbreaks, identify unfamiliar pathogens, and develop diagnostics and countermeasures. But that doesn't automatically cancel out an increase in offensive capability. A tool that helps develop a vaccine may also provide insights that are useful for causing harm. We need to evaluate those effects separately.

The goal, then, is to make defensive capabilities broadly useful while putting proportionate barriers around assistance that could materially enable serious biological harm. That means combining model safeguards with things like screening DNA synthesis orders and strengthening public health systems. It's a whole system problem; it won't be solved solely at the level of the model.
